Response operations. Thank you, Mr. President. Excellencies, 10 years ago, the 2030 Agenda recognized that a just and inclusive world demands women's equal voice in political and economic decision-making. While slow and uneven, progress has indeed been made. Global gender equality scores have risen by 2% since 2015, based on International IDEA's Global State of Democracy Indices. Within this overall trend lie important differences. Only 3% of democracies perform very poorly on gender equality measures, compared to 50% of authoritarian regimes. This shows clearly that democratic systems are better equipped to ensure equal rights and opportunities for all. However, despite these gains, the evidence underlines the scale of the challenges ahead. Women still hold only 27% parliamentary seats worldwide and 35% of local government positions. A new report by International IDEA also shows that women's freedom, freedom of discussion has decreased by 25%, and women's access to justice has dropped by over 12% globally. Rising authoritarianism, Online and offline gender-based violence, shrinking civic space, increased censorship, and institutional biases and impunity are the driving forces behind these declines. Despite these negative trends, International IDEA's report shows that several factors have contributed to the increase in gender equality scores in some countries, including the implementation of gender quotas in politics, the introduction of constitutional and legal reforms, and the adoption of new gender equality laws. Yet, let us be clear: the emancipation of women will not stop. Neither will the quest for more diverse, equitable, and inclusive societies. International IDEA will continue to do its part to leave no one behind and empower women and girls all over the world. Thank you.

Growing challenges such as conflict, humanitarian emergencies, and climate change continue to raise the death toll. Universal health coverage has hit a roadblock, with 4.5 million people still without essential health services and 2 billion facing financial hardship from out-of-pocket costs. The workforce shortages by 2030 have been readjusted up to 11.1 million, 2 million more from just 5 years ago. Efforts to combat communicable diseases to prevent millions of deaths are threatened by inequalities. Non-communicable diseases still continue to cause 75% of all deaths. Mental health conditions remain highly prevalent and often untreated. yet governments spend less than 2% of health budgets to mental health. Road traffic deaths remain a major global health and development challenge and leading cause of death for persons 5 to 29. Declining maternal mortality has also been a success story. On average, pregnancy and childbirth are becoming safer. But despite progress in immunization, there are still 14 million zero-dose children who never receive a single dose of any vaccine. Health is not created in the health sector, but how people live, eat, work, and learn. These determinants of health are only too clearly underscoring the significance of integrating a whole-of-society approach to policymaking and well-being. And to finance all of this.

Mr. President, the 2025 SDG report highlights the HIV response as an area of tangible progress. By 2024, new HIV infections had dropped by 61% and AIDS-related deaths by 70% from their peaks. This progress has both supported and benefited from broader SDG efforts: health, gender equality, education, and poverty reduction. The key has been global solidarity, multi-sectoral partnerships, and community-led, rights-based responses. But let us be clear: AIDS is not over. In 2024, there were 1.3 million new HIV infections, and more than 9 million people living with HIV had no access to treatment, leading to 630,000 AIDS-related deaths. 2025 was marked by sudden, large-scale funding cuts from international donors, with significant disruption in HIV treatment and prevention around the world. Adolescent girls, young women, and key populations are being particularly affected. UNAIDS estimates that the funding cuts could lead to an additional 6 million new HIV infections and 4 million AIDS-related deaths by 2029. Mr. President, the historic crisis requires a transformation to long-term programmatic, financial and political sustainability of the HIV response. 3 priorities stand out. Number one, national ownership and domestic financing must increase, supported by renewed global solidarity and donor commitment. Number 2, an HIV prevention revolution. Lenacapavir, a 6-month injectable pre-exposure prophylaxis, could be transformative if made available rapidly and affordably. Universal treatment access must also be maintained. And third, HIV integration with broader health systems, including universal health coverage and strengthened community-led responses and enabling legal and social environments. UNAIDS is doing its part to reform and support this transformation. We call on all stakeholders to step up to protect and sustain the hard-won gains.
